title: Visible repairs
bodyMd:
Original humanities exposition.

In the textile collection, a jacket with a bright triangular patch attracts more attention than several nearly flawless garments beside it. The patch was added long after the jacket was made. Its cloth does not match; its stitches are larger than the original seams. An early cataloger called the repair "clumsy" and placed the jacket in storage.

The current curator reads the patch differently. Fabric was costly in the mountain community where the jacket circulated, and garments often passed between family members. A conspicuous repair could signal neither carelessness nor poverty alone, but a decision to keep an object useful. The curator displays the jacket beside household accounts that list purchases of small pieces of cloth and payments for alterations.

The accounts do not identify this particular patch. They therefore cannot establish who repaired the jacket or why bright cloth was chosen. Their value is more modest: they show that alteration and reuse formed part of ordinary household practice. The jacket's repair becomes less anomalous when placed within that practice.

The new label retains the old cataloger's description, clearly attributed, alongside the curator's interpretation. Visitors can see how the same visible feature supports different judgments when evaluators ask different questions. The earlier cataloger assessed conformity to a presumed original appearance. The curator asks how an object remained useful over time. Neither the stitches nor the fabric changed while the jacket was in storage; the framework through which the museum viewed them did.
